input.topic: Before adding more AI steps, show me what they improve
input.audience: Professionals deciding how to use AI in their work
input.objective: Express Graham's practical skepticism about complexity and ask for observable usefulness. Make a clear, broadly relevant LinkedIn post, not a report about this software project or an explanation of tests. Use first-person judgment supported by the supplied conversation, without inventing a personal event, customer story, measurable saving or business result.

evidence.title: Graham's explicit direction in this conversation
evidence.fact: Graham questioned a proposed paid-API trial because an existing Codex subscription environment could be reused. He requested a quick, economical solution with extra layers deferred. This supports a preference for reusing what works and requiring complexity to earn its place; no savings have been measured.

evidence.title: Graham's actual reaction to the first comparison
evidence.fact: Graham said he preferred one draft, but called the test basic. He asked what had been used to generate it and what would be done with his answer. He requested an evaluation showing the brief, model context, changes made at each stage and final writing. Do not describe his preference as content approval or proof of superior quality.

engine.body:
I liked the AI draft. That proved very little.

I preferred one version, but I still wanted to know what had shaped it: the brief, the information the model had been given, and what each extra step changed in the final writing.

I also wanted to know what would happen with my preference. Would it inform a useful change, or just count as a vote for the winner?

That distinction matters when deciding how much AI to put into everyday work. Liking an answer is a useful signal. It doesn’t tell me which steps deserve the credit.

My starting point is to reuse what works and keep the process simple. If another step helps, show me where: a mistake caught, a clearer explanation, a requirement finally met.

I’m willing to add complexity. I want to see what it earns.

rewrite.body:
I preferred one AI draft. The process still had to earn its place.

The comparison was basic. I wanted to see the brief, the context given to the model, what changed at each stage, and the final writing. I also wanted to know what my preference would be used to change.

Picking a favourite answers one question. It doesn’t tell me which steps helped, or which were unnecessary.

That mattered when a paid-API trial was proposed. I already had a Codex subscription environment that could be reused, so I questioned the need for another route. I asked for a quick, economical solution, with extra layers deferred.

That wasn’t evidence of measured savings. It was a reason to make the case for adding something.

The same standard applies to the writing process. Show me the draft before a step and after it, alongside the requirement that step was meant to address. Then I can judge the change instead of giving the whole process credit for an answer I happen to like.

I’m willing to add complexity. My preference alone doesn’t justify it.
gaps: The paid-API detour introduces a second decision without making its connection to draft evaluation immediately clear.
The central distinction between liking an output and validating a process repeats more than it develops.
No concrete before-and-after writing example shows how the proposed evaluation would change a decision.
rewrite.rationale: The post offers a grounded, credible distinction between output preference and process value, with a useful evaluation method, but repetition and modest human stakes limit its impact.

visual_asset.rationale: Visual planning waits until the post has a publish-quality score at or above the configured threshold, so image/carousel work is not spent on a text candidate that still needs revision.

baseline.body:
Before adding more AI steps, show me what improves.

My first question is whether something I already have can do the job. If it can, I’d rather start there and leave the extra layers until there’s a reason to add them.

That’s practical skepticism, but I need to apply it to my own judgments too.

I can prefer one draft without knowing why it’s better, or whether the process behind it deserves any credit. A preference is a starting point. It doesn’t settle the question.

What was it asked to do? What information did it have? What did each extra step actually change?

Those questions matter when deciding how much AI to put into everyday work. Otherwise, it’s easy to add another review, another tool, another subscription, while still being unclear about what any of them contributes.

I want a clear reason to keep each addition: a mistake caught, a clearer answer, a result that better meets the brief. Something I can inspect, rather than just a more elaborate description of the process.

I’m open to more steps. I just want them to earn their place.

#AI #PracticalAI #FutureOfWork

source.role: primary historical voice authority explicitly authorized for reuse

guidance: Assume a smart reader who has never seen the internal project documents.
Translate internal methodology and repository vocabulary into ordinary language before using it.
For an individual Graham post, default to I/me/my; use we/us/our only for genuinely shared actions.
Make one main point per post and make the practical or human consequence clear.
Prefer concrete details supported by the evidence over abstract process language.
Do not force a CTA; a natural insight or earned provocation can be the ending.

runtime_guidance.style_summary: Write in a bold, witty, empathetic, direct and conversational voice with vivid but controlled imagery, varied sentence length, compact paragraphs, occasional dry humor, and a contrarian insight grounded in real stakes.
runtime_guidance.causal_summary: Move beyond the surface event. Explain what made it possible, what work breaks next, what cost or drag starts compounding, how trust or identity is affected, and what becomes harder to undo. Use only the layers that are actually supported by the topic and evidence.
runtime_guidance.domain_note: The original Voice Bible was developed heavily around cybersecurity. Preserve its voice and causal-thinking method across topics, but do not assume cybersecurity, C-suite buyers, or any specific professional identity unless the current request supplies that context.

spoken_voice.name: Graham Spoken Voice
spoken_voice.runtime_summary: Write as a thoughtful, plain-spoken Graham: curious before certain, direct without pretending every first impression is proven, conversational without transcribing filler, and willing to test his own argument before landing the point. Let the reasoning move from what happened, to what it may mean, to what it changes next. Use contrast, short declarative lines, occasional dry humor, and compact conclusions. Preserve the A-to-B-to-C instinct invisibly: show the current reality, the meaningful consequence, and the bridge or restraint that connects them. Do not over-explain. Do not sound like corporate copy. Do not turn private ENFP material into public biography.
boundaries: Do not infer biography, health, relationships, identity claims, or factual events from this schema.
Do not mention ENFP unless the current request/topic makes ENFP relevant.
Do not treat personality-type generalizations as evidence about Graham.
Do not reproduce private-source anecdotes unless they are separately supplied as factual evidence for the current post.
Do not imitate conversational filler words merely to sound informal.
composition_rules: Start from a concrete observation or tension rather than a generic thesis.
Let the reader see enough of the reasoning path to trust the conclusion.
Include one meaningful self-check or qualification when the claim genuinely needs it.
Move from the immediate event to the consequence that matters beyond Graham.
Land on a compact distinction, lesson, or earned question.
Keep the central point understandable to a smart outsider.
anti_patterns: sounding certain because certainty is rhetorically cleaner
over-explaining until the post feels like a defence brief
turning every insight into a framework acronym
repeating signature phrases as branding slogans
spoken_voice.signature_phrase_policy: These are conceptual anchors, not mandatory catchphrases. Use an exact phrase only when it fits naturally and is not being repeated across recent posts.
